Eleven years before Michael Jordan, Nike gave NBA star Spencer Haywood 10% of the company.

While Haywood was on a road trip, his agent sold the whole 10% stake for $100,000 in cash—just to collect his $10,000 fee.

In the video below, Haywood is asked if he is still friends with the man who sold it. His answer: "Yes."

In 1973, Haywood was 24 and averaging 29 points a game in Seattle. Phil Knight came to him and asked him to wear his new shoe.

Knight didn't have the cash to match Converse. So he offered Haywood stock instead.

"First of all, I was young, too, and I'm thinking: livestock? What are you talking about? Stocks," Haywood says.

Haywood took the stock.

His agent had a problem. An agent gets 10%. Ten percent of stock in a tiny shoe company couldn't pay his bills. Ten percent of $100,000 in cash was $10,000 in his pocket right away.

So the agent kept telling Haywood the shoe would never work. At the time, Nike only made running shoes for Steve Prefontaine. When Haywood ran down the court, defenders stepped on his heel and popped the shoe right off his foot.

Before leaving for a road trip, Haywood gave in.

"I said, 'Okay, man, I give you the power of attorney. Let me just go play. I got to really focus on this game now because this is my chance.'"

When Haywood came back, the stock was gone.

"He had sold that sh*t," Haywood says. "He said, 'Man, I got the cash right here — 100,000.'"

Matt Barnes asks him what that 10% of Nike would be worth.

"It was up around 2.7 billion," Haywood says. "Years ago." At Nike's peak, 10% was worth over $8.6 billion.

The case for the agent: in 1973, Nike was a tiny Oregon running-shoe company, and the shoes literally fell off Haywood's feet during games.

The Binance hacker might have just pulled off one of the smartest moves I’ve seen in crypto.

First, Tether froze $1.5 billion in USDT.

Then Circle froze another $800 million in USDC.

At that point, it looked like the hacker’s money was trapped.

But apparently, he had already planned for that.

Instead of holding the stolen USDT in a wallet, he allegedly deposited it into Aave and used it as collateral to borrow ETH.

Then he walked away.

That’s where the story gets crazy.

Tether can freeze the USDT sitting in the wallet.

But it can’t freeze the ETH he already borrowed.

So now Aave is left holding frozen collateral, while the hacker is sitting on liquid ETH.

And unless the protocol can recover it somehow, he may not even need to pay the loan back.

Two companies froze billions of dollars in seconds.

But someone who understood how to use DeFi may have found a way around both of them.

Pretty insane when you think about it.

Prince Naseem Hamed says his trainer Brendan Ingle, the man Pierce Brosnan plays in the film Giant, held him to a deal made when he was 11: £10 million once he had made £40 million. That is exactly the 25% Ingle took from his fighters' purses. They split in 1998, when Naseem was 24, and never made up before Ingle died in 2018.

In the video below, on talkSPORT as the film came out in January, Naseem says Ingle was "so money orientated, money motivated." Then the line he has carried since childhood: "You did a deal with me at 11 years old that you give me 10 million once you make 40 million." He adds that Ingle was "the highest paid trainer in the world."

Ingle told his side on camera years earlier, at 60, and it is the second half of the video. "I'm on 25% of whatever they get." When a fighter earns £400 and he takes £100, he says, nobody minds. "Then when I start getting them 40 grand," the mates start asking, "what are you giving him 10 grand for?"

He found Naseem at 7 in his gym in Wincobank, Sheffield, and walked him round the streets every Sunday night for 2 hours or more, talking about how he would become world champion. By the late 1990s Naseem was headlining Madison Square Garden, and the same quarter still came off every purse.

Ingle's camp says it was never greed. His sons advised on Giant, and Johnny Nelson, one of his world champions, says the old man had a van, wore no jewellery and never lived like a rich man. Naseem's only defeat came in 2001 against Marco Antonio Barrera, 3 years after he left the gym.

I think Ingle's own numbers explain the whole thing. 40 and 10 in his story, 40 and 10 in Naseem's, only the zeros changed. If anyone takes a percentage of what you earn, write down a ceiling or a review date while the sums are small, because that is the only time both sides find it easy to agree.

Pierce Brosnan's Ingle gets the last scene of the film, and Naseem says he only wishes it had been true. Was a quarter of a world champion's purses a fair price for 18 years of Sunday walks, or too much to hold a boy to for something he agreed at 11?

Marta Kostyuk’s 2026 season marked a clear step into the top tier, with a career-high ranking of No. 10, a maiden WTA 1000 title in Madrid, and consecutive major semifinals at Roland Garros and Wimbledon. Those results were driven by aggressive baseline play that produced high winner rates on both clay and hard courts, combined with improved consistency in longer rallies. At the French Open she ended a long clay-court win streak only in the semifinals against Mirra Andreeva; at Wimbledon she reached the last four for the first time, losing to Linda Nosková. The combination of first-time major depth and a 1000-level title moved her from perennial contender to a player capable of sustaining top-10 points across surfaces.
The limiting factor that emerged later in the year was physical rather than technical. A recurring wrist issue surfaced during the North American hard-court swing, forced her out of Beijing, and resurfaced in Ningbo, where she retired after losing the opening set to Ekaterina Alexandrova. That retirement ended any remaining chance of qualifying for the WTA Finals and confirmed that the same problem had already restricted her schedule. For a player whose game relies on heavy ball-striking and frequent first-strike opportunities, wrist durability directly affects both match volume and the ability to maintain the high-intensity patterns that produced her best results.
The practical question heading into 2027 is whether the Madrid and major-semifinal level can be repeated once the wrist is fully managed. Kostyuk has already shown she can convert strong weeks into ranking points at the highest level; the next test is whether she can string those weeks together across a full season without the interruptions that capped her 2026 campaign. If the physical issue remains controlled, her established ability to reach the second week of majors and win at the 1000 level gives her a clear path to remaining inside the top 10 rather than cycling in and out of it. https://t.co/blv4ffyvUJ
